# Impact of Nutritional Support for Tuberculosis on Intermediate and Terminal Undernutrition and Treatment Outcomes (INSTITUT) study: a protocol for a quasi-experimental study to assess the impact of nutritional support on tuberculosis treatment outcomes in Benin and Togo

**Authors:** Chelsie Cintron; Madolyn Dauphinais; Attannon Arnauld Fiogbe; Mohammed Fall Dogo; Safiou Ate; Christine Adjonou; Kokou Agossou; Susie Jiaxing Pan; Marius Esse; Benjamin Ade; Komi Séraphin Adjoh; Dissou Affolabi; Pranay Sinha; Kobto G Koura

**Affiliations:** 1Medicine - Infectious Diseases, Boston Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, Paris, Île-de-France, France | 3Programme National contre la Tuberculose, Cotonou, Benin | 4Unité de Suivi-Évaluation and Recherche, Programme National de Lutte Contre la Tuberculose, Lomé, Togo | 5Service de pneumologie, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sylvanus Olympio, Lome, Golfe, Togo | 6Section of Infectious Diseases, Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 7Sciences Pharmaceutiques et Biologiques, COMUE Sorbonne Paris Cité, Paris, France

## Abstract

Undernourished persons with tuberculosis (TB) (PWTB) are at increased risk of mortality, treatment failure and relapse. Nutritional support for PWTB has the potential to mitigate the risk of undernutrition. However, given ethical concerns, well-powered randomised control trials of macronutrient support are unavailable to inform policymakers, clinicians and researchers about the impact of nutritional support. However, there is potential to understand the impact of macronutrient nutritional support through a natural experiment. Benin and Togo are neighbouring countries in West Africa. Benin’s national TB programme currently provides all PWTB with nutritional support whereas Togo’s national TB programme does not provide nutritional support to PWTB with drug-susceptible strains. Comparing treatment outcomes of PWTB treated in Benin and Togo can help us understand the impact of nutritional support for PWTB.

We designed a programmatic, prospective cohort study to assess the treatment outcomes among persons with pulmonary tuberculosis under programmatic conditions. PWTB cared for in Benin served as the exposed populations and those in Togo served as control. We plan to enrol 1050 adult participants across two countries: 700 subjects from Benin and 350 from Togo. We did not alter nutritional services offered to PWTB for the purposes of this study. Participants will be identified by the National Tuberculosis Programs of each country through 13 basic management units and followed until 6 months after treatment completion. The outcome of interest is a composite of all-cause mortality, treatment failure and relapse. Additional secondary outcomes will assess the effects on the rate of sputum conversion, loss to follow-up, weight gain, quality of life and post-TB lung health using surveys and a 6 min walk test. We hypothesise that participants receiving nutritional support will experience fewer unfavourable outcomes, faster sputum clearance, improved weight gain and fewer persistent respiratory symptoms.

This study has received approval from the Boston University Medical Campus and Boston Medical Center Institutional Review Board (H-43096). The study also received a favourable decision from the Benin Comité d’Ethique de la Recherche and approval from the Comité de Bioéthique pour la Recherche en Santé of Togo. Informed consent will be obtained from all study participants prior to their engagement in the research. Findings from the study will be disseminated via national and international conferences and through manuscript publications in peer-reviewed journals. Data can be made available upon request to the corresponding author.

NCT06084715. Pre-results.

- The Impact of Nutritional Support for Tuberculosis on Intermediate and Terminal Undernutrition and Treatment Outcomes (INSTITUT) study is the first of its kind to capitalise on existing programmatic differences between two countries to assess the impact of nutritional support on tuberculosis (TB) outcomes.

- The INSTITUT study will provide an opportunity to conduct a quasi-experimental analysis of nutritional support for persons with TB (PWTB), which is challenging to do through traditional randomised studies because of the lack of adequate equipoise.

- To our knowledge, the INSTITUT study is the largest programmatic assessment of nutritional interventions for TB in West Africa to date.

- Differences in the quality of TB management approaches in Benin and Togo may confound our analysis.

- Food sharing and food consumption outside of that provided by Benin’s national TB programme are not accounted for.

## Background

Undernutrition is the primary risk factor for tuberculosis (TB) globally, with an estimated population attributable fraction of 19%, surpassing 7.6% for HIV and 3.1% for diabetes.1 2 Although nutritional rehabilitation may reverse the immunological deficits associated with undernutrition, efforts to address undernutrition as a risk factor fall behind those of HIV and diabetes among persons living with TB (PWTB) and other at-risk populations.3 COVID-19, natural disasters and global conflicts have exacerbated food insecurity worldwide, disproportionately affecting high TB burden countries.4 The United Nations reported that COVID-19 led to a sharp increase in undernutrition with an estimated 118 million more people experiencing hunger in 2020 than in 2019.5 Climate change further threatens nutritional stability as droughts, floods, hurricanes, wildfires and other natural disasters disrupt both agriculture and food distribution systems.6 Interruptions to food production threaten the food security of vulnerable populations in areas with forced migration from ongoing conflict.7

Undernutrition, including both macronutrient and micronutrient deficiencies, resulting from poor dietary intake is widely prevalent and often life-threatening among PWTB.8 Poor nutritional status is associated with increased TB disease severity, as evidenced by higher bacillary burdens in the sputum, greater lung involvement and greater risk of cavitation.911 Undernourished individuals may also experience decreased drug absorption or increased drug toxicity.12 A large study in India found that each unit increase in baseline body mass index (BMI) was correlated with a 22% (95% CI 10% to 32%) reduction in mortality.13 Moreover, the inability to gain weight during the intensive phase of therapy is a marker for treatment failure, relapse and mortality.1416 These data underscore the significance of nutritional status on TB outcomes, and although the relationship between undernutrition and TB is bidirectional, the association between undernutrition and poor outcomes remains robust even after adjusting for confounders.

A systematic review of macronutrient supplementation for PWTB found evidence supporting nutritional interventions in promoting weight gain and accelerating sputum clearance.17 However, the results from this review are limited by the small sample size and heterogeneity. Some likely provided insufficient nutrients to detect an impact on critical TB-specific outcomes, such as mortality. Nonetheless, due to historical and contemporary data, there is insufficient equipoise to justify randomised controlled studies of providing nutritional support to persons with TB.3 4 The Impact of Nutritional Support for Tuberculosis on Intermediate and Terminal Undernutrition and Treatment Outcomes (INSTITUT) study hopes to address this lacuna by taking advantage of a natural experiment unfolding in Benin and Togo.

The Benin national TB programme currently offers programmatic nutritional support to all PWTB. In contrast, Togo’s national TB programme lacks a nutritional support component. The INSTITUT study aims to prospectively compare treatment outcomes across countries to understand the impact of programmatic in-kind nutritional support on nutritional recovery, treatment outcomes and post-TB lung health in West Africa.

## Methods

### Aims, objectives and outcomes

The INSTITUT project has two primary aims and outcomes: (1) to estimate the impact of nutritional support on TB treatment failure, death or relapse and (2) to estimate the impact of nutritional support on the nutritional status of PWTB at the end of treatment. The secondary aims of INSTITUT are to assess the effects of nutritional supplementation on the rate of sputum smear conversion at 2 months, weight gain during treatment (5% weight gain at 2 months; BMI at the end of treatment), quality of life and post-TB lung health as captured by persistent pulmonary symptoms and a 6-minute walk test. We hypothesise that participants receiving nutritional support will experience fewer unfavourable outcomes, faster sputum clearance, improved weight gain and fewer persistent respiratory symptoms.

### Study design and setting

The INSTITUT study is a programmatic, prospective cohort analysis conducted in national tuberculosis programme (NTP) hospitals in Benin and Togo in partnership with the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease and Boston Medical Center. The Republic of Benin has six data collection sites: (1) Basic Management Unit (BMU) Lazaret (National Teaching Hospital for TB and Respiratory Diseases (CNHU-PPC)), (2) BMU Calavi, (3) BMU Sèmè-Podji, (4) Godomey, (5) Akron and (6) Bethesda. The Togolese Republic has seven data collection sites: (7) Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sylvanus Olympio (CHU SO), (8) BMU Adidogomé, (9) BMU Agoe Nyive, (10) Polyclinique Demakpoe, (11) Cs N’kafu, (12) Hopital de Be and (13) Centre de Sante Adakpame. 12 field teams of charge nurses, healthcare workers and a research assistant (Benin only) are responsible for study enrolment and participant follow-up. Enrolment began in September and November 2023 in Togo and Benin, respectively.

### Study population

Benin and Togo are neighbouring West African countries which are well suited for this study due to their demographic, socioeconomic and cultural similarities, which support meaningful comparisons. According to the World Bank, both countries have comparable population sizes, life expectancies and population growth rates.18 The GINI index—a measure of income inequality—is similar, with Benin at 34.4 and Togo at 37.9. Both countries also have similar TB incidence rates (Benin at 52/100 000 and Togo at 32/100 000) and receive financial and technical support from the WHO and the Global Fund for TB programmes.2 Additionally, both nations share overlapping ethnic and tribal groups, with individuals from the same cultural regions residing across borders, contributing to comparable dietary practices. These similarities ensure that participants from both countries can be meaningfully compared, though any residual differences will be addressed through appropriate statistical adjustments in our analysis. Moreover, both countries have similarly structured national TB programmes that have identical treatment protocols and frequently collaborate with each other.

We are enrolling persons with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB who receive care at BMUs of NTP hospitals in Benin and Togo. Inclusion criteria are as follows: (1) age 18 years or older; (2) drug susceptible, GeneXpert MTB-RIF (Xpert) positive, and/or sputum smear positive (≥1+ acid-fast bacilli (AFB)); and (3) willing to attend follow-up visits and undergo study procedures. Exclusion criteria are as follows: (1) drug-resistant TB; (2) having received 7 or more days of antimicrobial therapy; (3) being too sick to enrol as defined as a score of 4 on the WHO Performance Status per study staff observation; (4) being pregnant at the time of enrolment; and (5) being unable to complete 6-min walk test due to pre-existing mobility issues due to disability, trauma, neurological compromise or cardiopulmonary disease. Enrolment is open to individuals with extrapulmonary TB; however, they must have evidence of pulmonary involvement to be eligible. To calculate power, we assumed that 10% of individuals not receiving nutritional support die or show evidence of treatment failure prior to end of therapy and approximately 5% of individuals would experience those outcomes. Further, we planned a 1:2 ratio between unexposed and exposed arms. To attain a power of 80% to detect this difference, we would need 334 unexposed participants and 676 exposed participants. In anticipation of 10% of participants withdrawing from the study, we increased our recruitment goals to 350 unexposed in Togo and 700 exposed participants in Benin. We expect to enrol 1050 subjects in total (figure 1).

*Figure 1: The Impact of Nutritional Support for Tuberculosis on Intermediate and Terminal Undernutrition and Treatment Outcomes (INSTITUT) study schematic.*

### Patient and public involvement

This is a programmatic study being conducted internally within the Programme National contre la Tuberculose (PNT) in Benin and the Programme National de Lutte contre la Tuberculose (PNLT) in Togo. As such, we did not partake in community engagement efforts. Ethical approvals were put in place to ensure that our research was consistent with the values of the participating countries. However, we plan to disseminate our findings to key community partners as well as the general public in addition to publishing our findings in academic journals.

### Study procedures, assessments and schedule

#### Consent and eligibility screening

PWTB are approached for study enrolment and consented in private at the BMU during their initial visit for TB care. Participants engage in extensive discussions of study objectives, procedures, and the risks and benefits of study participation with study staff before consenting to participate. Written informed consent is obtained from all participants prior to the performance of any study procedures. Staff conduct laboratory evaluation of sputum for nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) by Cepheid’s GeneXpert19 and AFB culture, chest radiograph (CXR), and a urine pregnancy test to determine eligibility status in women of childbearing age. NAAT results are obtained from medical records, and if unavailable at the time of enrolment, NAAT testing is performed. Sputum microscopy is performed on all participants, though subject to the participant’s ability to produce sputum. Chest radiography is completed at baseline if an X-ray has not been conducted previously. Women receive a urine pregnancy test prior to the CXR to prevent potential fetal radiation exposure. Medical history, socioeconomic status, and height and weight for BMI are collected in addition to the 6 min walk assessment. Height is measured using stadiometers and weight is measured using digital scales. Measurement has been standardised across all study sites with uniform equipment and calibration. The study team reviews all assessments and evaluation instruments in conjunction to determine participant eligibility using the study criteria.

#### Demographics, medical history and physical assessments

Demographic information is collected at baseline and during follow-up visits (months 2, 6 and 12). We collect information regarding socioeconomic status (global multidimensional poverty index)20 at baseline, alcohol consumption (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-C))21 at baseline, and quality of life (EuroQol 5 Dimension (EQ-5D))22 at baseline and follow-up visits (months 2, 6 and 12), as these factors may link to TB infection. Participants also complete a chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) assessment23 at baseline and during follow-up visits (months 6 and 12).

#### Follow-up visits

Participants complete three follow-up visits after baseline: months 2, 6 and 12. Month 6 visit is conducted at the time of TB treatment completion, while month 12 visit is conducted 6 months post-treatment completion. During the month 2 visit, study staff conduct a sputum smear for those who can produce sputum. Study staff assess quality of life (EQ-5D) and medication adherence via pill counts and inspection of TB medication blister packs. Participants’ height and weight are reassessed for BMI determination. Through the national TB programme (NTP), Benin sites provide participants with nutritional supplementation.

During the month 6 and month 12 visits, study staff assess medical history, quality of life (EQ-5D), medication adherence via pill counts, and inspection of TB medication blister packs (month 6 only). Staff also administer a COPD assessment. We conduct a physical assessment of height and weight measurements for BMI determination as well as a 6 min walk assessment. Additionally, at the month 12 visit, participants receive a post-treatment CXR and we determine their final treatment outcome. Table 1 depicts study visit procedures.

### Benin nutritional supplementation

Benin’s NTP provides country-wide nutritional support to all PWTB. All persons with drug-susceptible TB are eligible for nutritional support through Benin’s national TB programme. The national nutrition programme is funded jointly by The Global Fund and the Government of Benin, though the government of Benin assumes two-thirds of the cost. The supplement, outlined in table 2, includes but not limited to components such as spaghetti, corned beef, powdered cassava (garri), condensed milk with sugar, sardines, sugar cubes, red beans, white beans, tomato paste, onions and sorghum (cereal grain). As there is no fixed food ration, the provided food basket comprises a rotation of the aforementioned food items for outpatient participants. The food type and quantity provided to PWTB are subject to the availability of ingredients and the BMU location. The frequency of food receipt is also variable dependent on availability. At most, PWTB will receive biweekly baskets and at minimum, once monthly. Hospitalised PWTH at Akron and Lazaret BMUs receive prepared meals three times per day.

### Data management

#### Data collection

All data are coded using participant identification numbers to maintain confidentiality. A designated study team member manually reviews the paper case report forms for completion and quality. A designated data coordinator is responsible for entering hardcopy data from paper forms into the online database, EpiData V.3.1.

#### Quality control

The investigational site is responsible for conducting routine quality assurance and quality control activities to internally monitor study progress and protocol compliance. The principal investigator and/or designated staff monitor these activities. Data checks are built into EpiData while a designated staff member also verifies digital data by reviewing electronic data against paper copies. We use this process to confirm the validity of the provided responses. We return any identified inconsistencies or incomplete forms to the field team for rectification. In addition, the Boston team performs routine data analysis and audits to evaluate the completion and consistency of data. Regular query reports are sent to the local teams and the team periodically visits the study sites to oversee data collection and entry.

#### Statistical analyses

The primary exposure is receipt of nutritional support which is limited to the Benin sites. The primary outcome will be a composite variable of unfavourable outcomes, including TB treatment failure, death or relapse based on evaluation 12 months after treatment initiation. An additional primary outcome will be BMI at the end of treatment and 1 year after treatment initiation. Secondary outcomes will be (1) sputum smear conversion at 2 months, (2) loss to follow-up during therapy, (3) quality of life as measured by EQ-5D score and (4) severity of post-TB chronic lung disease as captured by the validated COPD assessment test, degree of scarring on post-treatment chest radiograph, and 6 min walk test.

We will consider a comprehensive list of confounders including demographic factors (age, sex, urban vs rural residence), socioeconomic factors (multidimensional poverty index), disease-related risk factors (sputum smear grade, cavitation, cough duration, adherence, use of directly observed treatment, duration of hospitalisation, treatment support with community health workers), and comorbidities (BMI at start of treatment, HIV status and CD4 level, diabetes history, alcohol use, and tobacco use).

We will generate descriptive statistics for the primary dependent and independent variables as well as covariates. We will then pursue univariate analysis. χ2 analysis will be used for categorical variables and logistic regression will be used for continuous variables (age and years of education). We will calculate the variance inflation factor and set the cut-off at 5. We will remove redundant variables and possibly aggregate variables if appropriate. Finally, we will proceed with multivariable analysis with logistic regression. Age, sex and cough duration will be included in the multivariable analysis a priori. All covariates which are significant at p=0.2 will be included as well. We also plan a subgroup analysis of individuals in Benin who receive food only during the intensive phase and those who receive food through the entirety of their treatment. Additionally, we will apply causal inference techniques to address selection bias and strengthen the validity of our findings. Specifically, we will use propensity score matching to create balanced comparison groups between participants from Benin and Togo based on key baseline characteristics.

### Study expectations

In this study, we hypothesise that the risk of treatment failure or mortality is 50% lower among PWTB receiving nutritional support. Further, we hypothesise that the risk of remaining undernourished after TB treatment (defined as BMI <18.5 kg/m2) is 50% lower among those receiving nutritional support. We expect to quantify the impact of nutritional support on TB treatment outcomes. We anticipate that participants receiving nutritional supplementation as part of their TB care will have more favourable treatment outcomes compared with those who do not receive nutritional supplementation, faster sputum conversion, improved quality of life and less post-TB lung disease. Data from this study will allow us to inform TB policies by potentially identifying high-risk patient groups and improving disease management strategies throughout treatment.

## Discussion

The INSTITUT study allows us to assess the impact of nutrition on TB across two national TB programmes and gather data to inform the integration of nutritional supplementation in TB care locally and globally. Studying the impact of nutritional support on treatment outcomes using randomised clinical trials is ethically fraught as there is insufficient equipoise, particularly in light of the recent Reducing Activation of Tuberculosis by Improvement of Nutrition Status study24 as well as previously conducted interventional studies. The INSTITUT study offers a quasi-experimental alternative to answer this critical question by capitalising on the current differences in the nutritional support offered in Benin and Togo which have comparable health systems and populations.

One strength of this study is the strong partnership with TB programmes in adjacent, comparable countries allowing for a natural programmatic comparison and to implement testable hypotheses in a large population. The well-established nutritional programme in Benin is key to our understanding of the impact nutritional supplementation has on TB outcomes when compared with Togo’s programme which currently does not provide nutritional support. Further, within Benin, select BMUs provide extensive nutritional counselling alongside the food basket programme. We are positioned to understand the interplay of nutritional programmes, alone and in combination with nutritional counselling on TB outcomes. Our analyses also allow us to understand the effect of nutritional support on the nutritional recovery and quality of life of PWTB and whether nutritional support has potential as a host-directed therapy for post-TB chronic lung disease.

The study does have some potential weaknesses. This is a programmatic study that disallowed us from collecting large amounts of socio-demographic data. We also were unable to facilitate spirometry to assess for post-TB chronic lung disease outcomes and had to rely on validated survey data. Nutritional support provided in Benin is also not uniform across participants as it is provided ad hoc by the programme. We did not alter the nutritional composition of the programme as this was a programmatic study. The study design and financial limitations of the nutritional programme may result in dietary inconsistencies that will need to be accounted for during data analysis. Although we will employ causal inference methods to strengthen the analysis, the non-randomised nature of the study limits the extent to which we can draw definitive causal conclusions.

We expect that the provision of food will affect participants through numerous mechanisms, such as improving their food security, enhancing their immune response to TB, limiting drug toxicity and improving their adherence to TB medications.4 25 However, as this is a programmatic study, we are limited in the amount of data we can collect. While we do have records about the receipt of food baskets and the number of months individuals received support, we are not able to collect data on the number of calories consumed. Further, we acknowledge that participants may not consume the supplied food as intended and that provided food baskets are not the sole source of nutrition. Collecting dietary data through tools such as 24-hour recalls and food frequency questionnaires is labour intensive and, therefore, not possible in our study context. In addition, dietary records typically require literacy, which is not guaranteed among all study participants. Our study is designed to show that a policy action in terms of providing in-kind nutritional support may improve both nutritional and treatment outcomes. Additional mixed-methods research is crucial to understand the mechanisms by which such policy action can have its desired effect.

Currently, there is a paucity of data on the impact of nutritional support on TB treatment outcomes, particularly TB mortality and funding for TB—undernutrition research has been historically underfunded.26 The majority of the available evidence comes from India, which is a distinct epidemiological population with a lower rate of HIV.25 27 To catalyse policy change in West Africa, it is critical to generate local data on the impact of nutritional support programmes on TB outcomes. Doing so in a programmatic setting is also crucial as this provides a real-world assessment of effectiveness as opposed to efficacy in controlled experimental settings. This is the rationale behind our study. Further, this project directly supports South-South cooperation that allows two countries with expertise in TB care and nutritional support for PWTB to drive the creation and sharing of best practices for TB care across West African countries. Demonstration of a positive impact of nutritional support would provide a powerful impetus for implementing in-kind nutritional support in other African TB programmes. Indeed, evidence generated through the INSTITUT can be rapidly disseminated through close-knit networks such as the West and Central African Regional Network for TB control and has the potential to influence integration of nutritional care in TB programmes across the African continent.

### Ethics and dissemination

This study has received approval from the Boston University Medical Campus and Boston Medical Center Institutional Review Board (H-43096). The study also received a favourable decision from the Benin Comité d’Ethique de la Recherche and approval from the Comité de Bioéthique pour la Recherche en Santé of Togo. Informed consent will be obtained from all study participants prior to their engagement in the research. Findings from the study will be disseminated via national and international conferences and through manuscript publications in peer-reviewed journals. Data can be made available upon request to the corresponding author.

## Data availability statement

Data are available upon reasonable request.
